History of Uzbekistan, code CC-MOHU010106, Tashkent Technological University,
Faculty of Power Engineering.
Compulsory module, 4 ECTS, autumn semester
2026/2027; coordinator — Dr Vohid Kholov. Workload: 30 contact hours of lectures
(2 h per week, 15 weeks) + 90 hours of independent work = 120 hours.
Assessment: Midterm — written, 1–2 hours, 30% (ILOs 1–5); project presentation
— written and oral, 10–15 minutes, 20%; final exam — written, 1–2 hours, 50%.
Scale: 90 −100 = A (excellent), 75 −89 = B(good), 60 −74 = C(satisfactory), 0 −59 =
D(unsatisfactory). Attendance of at least 75% of classes is required for admission to
the final exam.
Planned learning outcomes (ILOs): (1) Understanding — explain the basic concepts
of history, statehood, and the role of science and technology in the development of
the country; (2) Analysis — analyze Uzbekistan’s contemporary policy in retrospect;
(3) Selection — select qualitative and quantitative data and the methods of Orien-
talism, oral history, source analysis, hermeneutics, anchoring in place and time; (4)
Evaluation — judge political changes and reforms: openness and transparency, a
multi-vector foreign policy, socially oriented policy; (5) Application — work in small
groups on projects and present historical processes in writing and orally.

2 2. Week 1 — The Subject Matter of History
Week files: Lecture_I__The_subject_matter_of_History.doc · The_subject_matter_of_
History.pptx
Week 1 answers the questions: what is history as a science and as an academic
discipline, what is its nature, which types and auxiliary disciplines are included in it,
how primary sources differ from secondary ones, and by which methods historians
verify the reliability of information. Below are gathered all the propositions, all the
questions (savollar), all the tests (testlar) and all the terms (atamalar) based on the
materials of the lecture and the slides.
2.1 2.1. Key points (the “all the rules” of the week)
The definition of history and its «raw material»
History — the study of the life of society in the past in all its aspects, in connection
with the present and the expectations of the future; it is the story of man in time, an
inquiry into the past on the basis of evidence. Evidence/fact is the «raw material»
of teaching and studying history. History is an attempt to re-think the past: what
happened, when and how.
The aim of the module is to help the student understand the modern social, political,
religious and economic conditions of people’s lives: without knowledge of history
there is no basis for understanding religion, customs, institutions and governance.
History reveals cause-and-effect connections between the past and the present and
makes it possible to understand problems at the national and international level ac-
curately and objectively.
Key quotations about history (the authors must be known)
Burckhardt: «History is the record of what one age finds worthy of note in another».
Henry Johnson: «History in its widest sense is everything that has ever happened».
Smith, V.S: «The value and interest of history depend on the extent to which the
present is illuminated by the past».
Rapson: «History is a connected account of the course of events or of the progression
of ideas».
NCERT: «History is the scientific study of past events in all aspects of the life of a
social group in the light of what is happening in the present».
Jawaharlal Nehru: «History is the story of man’s struggle through the ages against
nature and the elements; against wild beasts and the jungle and against those of his
own kind who tried to keep him down and exploit him».
Alisher Navoi: from history we know which ruler was cruel and who held the banner
of justice; the qualities and shortcomings of every person are recorded in history.
Ibrat: knowledge of the history of the homeland is necessary for every inhabitant.

Abdurauf Fitrat: «History is the subject that studies the causes of the prosperity and
the crisis of our people in the past».
Additional (slides): Voltaire — «History is the study of all the crimes of the world»;
Robert Heinlein — «A generation which ignores history has no past and no future»;
Confucius — «Study history, study history: in history lie all the secrets of statecraft»;
Napoleon — «History is a set of lies agreed upon»; Richard Paul Evans — «The more
I study history, the more clearly I see how little humanity has changed: there are no
new scenarios, only different actors».
The nature of history (11 propositions of the lecture)
1) The study of the present in the light of the past: the present has grown out of
the past; causal connections are restored.
2) History is the science of man: the
story of man’s struggle through the ages, of how man learned to use and control his
environment. 3) History is concerned with man in time: every event takes place at
a definite moment of time, time gives perspective. 4) History is concerned with man
in space: the interaction of man and his environment; politics, society, the economy
and culture grow out of the geographical context.
5) An objective record of events: the data are built on primary sources and freed
from subjective interpretation. 6) Many-sidedness: historical events cover all sides
of life, not only the political one. 7) History is a dialogue between the events of the
past and the gradually emerging ends of the future; on the basis of general laws
attempts are made to forecast the future. 8) Not only narration but also analysis:
causal connections are uncovered, general laws are formulated and compared with
other societies.
9) Continuity and coherence are the necessary conditions of history: human progress
is handed down from generation to generation. 10) Relevance: only events impor-
tant for the understanding of modern life are included. 11) All-comprehensiveness:
history is not limited to one period, one country or one nation and embraces the po-
litical, social, economic, religious, literary, aesthetic and physical sides of life — a
sense of world unity.
Three key points for understanding the essence of history
Experience — a combination of positive and negative notions about man or the his-
torical process, their analysis and interpretation. Thought — an idea or a point of
view formed out of many facts: a preponderance of negative facts forms a negative
thought, and vice versa. Fact/Evidence — the raw material of history: the study of
what happened, when and how.
The most important conclusion of the lecture: contrary to common opinion, the most
important thing is EXPERIENCE, then thought, and only then fact. The knowledge
of many facts by itself does not mean the knowledge of history: without facts history
turns into literature, but facts are merely instruments leading to reality.
The example of T. Welsford (Oxford): in the Samarkand archive a document of a
petitioner to the qadi (judge) against a brother who would not divide the paternal
land makes it possible to call the brother a bad man; but a second document shows
that the brother offered his brother half the value of the land so that the latter could
buy land elsewhere or take up trade — the income from the land was sufficient for
only one family. Conclusion: one source distorts, several sources create an objective
picture.
The role of the interpretant: «history is written by the victors». Governments and
funds pay for the writing of history and want to read it the way they imagine it; his-

torians depended on rulers. Therefore it is necessary to compare different data from
different sources. Example: the colonizers justified invasions by «the introduction
to civilization»; today the same processes are described by the words «democracy»,
«human rights», «feminism».
The example of Amir Timur (Timur): under Soviet rule he was studied mostly nega-
tively under the influence of ideology, while in the years of independence his status
was raised to that of a national hero — research showed that he developed trade,
architecture, international relations and science. Similarly Genghis Khan: for us —
a barbarian conqueror who ravaged flourishing cities, for the Mongols — a hero.
Conclusion: the assessment of a historical figure depends on the position of the in-
terpreter.
«Knowing history» versus «doing history»; types of history
Knowing history — the accumulation of information, «walking encyclopedias», col-
lectors of facts «in a cupboard of knowledge». Doing history — interrogating the
past in order to make sense of the world; historical research and historical thinking:
working with competing versions and narratives, understanding «strangers in time»,
even if they are not strangers in space.
Types of history (slides): political, diplomatic, social, intellectual, cultural, economic
history.
Disciplines included in history
Archaeology — the scientific study of the material remains of past human life: from
the most ancient stone tools to modern discarded objects; from dwellings, tem-
ples and tombs to palaces and pyramids. The word comes from the Greek archaia
(«antiquities»)+ logos («teaching»). The archaeologist first describes and classifies
the finds (objective taxonomy is the foundation of archaeology), but the main goal
is to place the material remains in a historical context; in the end the archaeologist
is a historian. Over 150 years large local and international excavations have been
carried out in Central Asia, which have revealed the way of life, the origins, the trade
and the economy of the region.
Ethnography and ethnology — from the Greek ethnos («people»)+ graphein («to
write»); according to Wolcott (1999) this is the description of the «ordinary social
behaviors» of a recognizable group of people. Ethnographers use the method of par-
ticipant observation: the anthropologist studies the life of a group by taking part in its
activities. Ethnological research is the «intellectual antivirus» of society: it cleanses
it of rumors and superstitions (for example, the prohibition of washing floors at night,
and the like).
Source studies — «trust but verify»: the authenticity of the information is deter-
mined, as well as the behaviour of the author, the language of the source, the charac-
ter of the source, the style of writing; language changes, words change their meaning
or fall out of use.
Historiography — the study of the methods of historians in developing history as an
academic discipline; any body of historical work on a particular subject. Examples of
subjects: the historiography of the Central Asian renaissance, of the Second World
War, of the Middle Ages, of early Islam; genres include political and social history.
Since the 19th century (with the development of academic history) a historiograph-
ical literature has taken shape; the question of the influence of the loyalties of the
historian (for example, to the nation state) remains debatable.
Chronology — the science of the arrangement of historical events in time; it relies

on chronometry (the measurement of time) and historiography. Its main task is the
synchronization of events: to connect an event with the current time and to compare
it with other events; a typical task is the synchronization of the reigns of tsars and
rulers of different countries.
Numismatics — the scientific analysis of money and of the ways it has been used
in history; also the collecting of coins, banknotes, tokens and medals. Numismatics
helps to study the history of money, culture (symbols on coins), religion and beliefs,
rulers and their times, the history of relations, metallurgy, mining, chemistry, draft-
ing, physics and more.
Historical methodologies (techniques of presenting information)
Palaeography — the study of historical handwriting; diplomatics — the study of doc-
uments; the study of records and archives; chronology — the establishment of the
dates of past events; the study of publications; epigraphy — the study of ancient
inscriptions; genealogy — the study of people and families; historical geography;
heraldry — the study of coats of arms and weapons; codicology — the study of hand-
written books; numismatics — coins; sphragistics — the study of seals; the study of
new media (historical digital literacy).
Primary and secondary sources
Primary sources — documents or artifacts created by a witness of or a participant in
an event; testimonies created during the period under study. The list of the lecture:
manuscripts and archival materials; books and pamphlets; data; dissertations and re-
search results; ephemeral printed matter (cards, tickets, labels, as well as banknotes
and marriage certificates); government documents; maps; objects and artifacts; oral
history; magazines, newspapers and scholarly journals; sound recordings and visual
materials. The collection and analysis of primary sources is the central part of his-
torical research.
Secondary sources — created considerably later than the events described, or by a
person who took no part in the events and was not their eyewitness; they include
simple descriptions of primary sources without verbatim reproduction. These are
books and articles on the subject, often with lists of sources (a bibliography) leading
to other primary and secondary sources.
The historian’s methods: source criticism and synthesis
Source criticism / information evaluation — the process of evaluating the quality of
a source: validity, reliability, relevance to the subject.
Procedures for contradic-
tory sources; principles for determining reliability; the testimonies of eyewitnesses;
indirect witnesses; oral tradition; anonymous sources.
Five basic questions to ask of a source: When was the source created (date)? Where
was it created (localization)?
By whom was it created (authorship)?
From what
original material was it created (analysis)? In what original form (integrity)? What
is the evidential value of its content (credibility)?
Synthesis — historical reasoning: objectivity, causality, chronology, historical con-
text; the techniques are the «argument to the best explanation» and statistical infer-
ence.
2.2 2.2. Savollar — lecture questions with model answers
S1. What is the conceptual benefit of studying history?
7

Answer. History helps to explain the present: without knowledge of the past there is
no basis for understanding religion, customs, institutions and governance. It devel-
ops analytical skills and critical thinking, forms an «intellectual immunity» in discus-
sions, teaches how to reveal cause-and-effect connections between the past and the
present and how to assess national and international problems objectively. History
is the foundation of all the humanities and social sciences, of philosophy, politics,
economics, art and religion; different interpretations of the past allow one to see the
present differently and to work for different versions of the future.
S2. Give quotations about history.
Answer. One must be able to give at least 2–3 quotations with their authors: Bur-
ckhardt — «the record of what one age finds worthy of note in another»; Henry
Johnson — «everything that has ever happened»; Rapson — «a connected account of
the course of events or the progression of ideas»; NCERT — «the scientific study of
past events in the light of the present»; Nehru — «the story of man’s struggle against
nature and against oppressors of his own kind»; Navoi — history shows who was a
cruel ruler and who held the banner of justice; Ibrat — knowledge of the history of
the homeland is necessary for everyone; Fitrat — history studies the causes of the
prosperity and the crisis of our people; Voltaire, Confucius, Napoleon, Heinlein —
additionally (see the rules section).
S3. What is necessary in order to study and research history?
Answer. Facts-evidence from primary and secondary sources are necessary, as well
as the knowledge of the methods: source criticism (date, localization, authorship,
analysis of the material, integrity, credibility) and synthesis (objectivity, causality,
chronology, context). Comparative and analytical skills are needed: to compare dif-
ferent sources about one event, to take into account the role of the interpretant
(«history is written by the victors»), to distinguish facts, thoughts and experience,
where experience is the summit. The auxiliary disciplines are useful — archaeology,
numismatics, chronology, source studies, ethnology, historiography.
S4. Which subjects (disciplines) are included in history?
Answer. Archaeology — the study of the past through excavations; chronology —
the study of time and calendars; source studies — the study of written sources; nu-
mismatics — the study of coins; ethnology — the study of traditions; plus histori-
ography as the study of the methods of historians. The methodologies also include
palaeography, diplomatics, epigraphy, genealogy, heraldry, codicology, sphragistics
and historical geography.
S5. What are the differences between primary and secondary sources?
Answer. A primary source was created by an eyewitness or a participant of an event
during the period under study (manuscripts, archives, documents, maps, oral his-
tory, the contemporary press, artifacts).
A secondary source was created consid-
erably later than the event or by a person who took no part in it, and analyzes a
scholarly question relying on primary sources (books and articles, bibliographies).
The rules for secondary sources are simpler: they are always «after» the event and
often describe primary sources without reproducing them verbatim.

3 3. Week 2 — Central Asian Civilization and Early Tech-
nological Achievements
Week files: Lecture_II__Central_Asain_Civilization.doc · Lecture_II__2_.pptx
Week 2 proves that Turan/Turkestan is an integral part of world civilization: settled
life, cities, art and irrigation arose here independently. One needs to know the con-
cept of civilization, the Neolithic and Bronze Age cultures, the Neolithic Revolution

and the waves of migrations. Below — all the propositions, questions, tests and terms
of the lecture and the slides.
3.1 3.1. Key points (the “all the rules” of the week)
The concept of civilization
Civilization — a complex human society, usually made up of different cities, with
certain characteristics of cultural and technological development; an advanced state
of human society with highly developed forms of government, culture, industry and
common social norms. The word is connected with the Latin civitas («city»), so the
basic definition is «a society made up of cities».
The best-known world civilizations: Egyptian, Babylonian, Chinese, Indian, Greco-
Roman, Arab.
However, the newest archaeological research in Central Asia has
proved that the ancient development of the region is one of the centers of world
civilization, which has been recognized by prominent world scholars. The term «civ-
ilization» was often used ethnocentrically: «civilizations» were considered morally
good and advanced, the rest — backward; therefore the definition remains debatable
to this day.
The concept of Central Asia
The concept of «Central Asia» was first introduced into scholarship by A. von Hum-
boldt in the 19th century during his journeys across the region. It should not be
confused with Central Eurasia, which occupies a larger territory. Central Asia is a
vast territory, also called Turkestan in the sources; it is almost the same geographical
space: from Uyghuria to the Caspian basin, from the south of Siberia to Iran. The
present geographical position of Central Asia is part of historical Turkestan, also
known as Turan.
Politically, Central Asia embraces the territories of Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzs-
tan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan. In Soviet times the region was called «Middle Asia
and Kazakhstan»; after the dissolution of the USSR all these countries came to be
called Central Asia.
Early life and culture: the Palaeolithic and the Mesolithic
The occupation of the region began as early as the Lower Palaeolithic.
Sources
of knowledge: petroglyphs (rock drawings), wall paintings, tools of stone. In the
Mesolithic the bow and arrows appeared — an important technological achievement
of the epoch.
The Neolithic and Neolithic cultures
The 6th–5th millennia BC — the «revolution of mankind» (the Neolithic Revolution):
the transition to an appropriating-and-producing economy almost simultaneously
with Western Asia. There appear: the first settled economy, new branches of the
economy, the building of houses, early crafts, settled agriculture, hunting and fish-
ing, cattle breeding; comfortable houses with neat finishing, bright pottery, the wide
use of ornament. This qualitative leap prepared the base for the creation of the an-
cient civilizations. At the same time the development was uneven: the tribes of Iran
and southern Turkmenistan passed to the new forms of economy earlier, in other
areas the transition was delayed; hunters, fishers and gatherers coexisted with the
settled communities of the oases.

Jeitun (Djeitun) — a Neolithic site in southern Turkmenistan; settled approximately
in 7200-4500 BC with possible short interruptions. It gave its name to the whole
Neolithic period of the foothills of the Kopet Dag. Sheep and goats had already been
domesticated, but the inhabitants supplemented their diet by hunting. Here, for the
first time in the region, agriculture developed.
Kelteminar — a Neolithic culture of 5500-3500 BC of settled fishers of the semi-
deserts and deserts of the Karakum and the Kyzylkum, the deltas of the Amu Darya
and the Zeravshan. Named after the Kelteminar site; replaced by the Tazabagyab
culture. People lived in huge houses (24×17m, up to 10 m high) where the whole clan
community of 100–120 people lived; they adorned themselves with beads of shells;
they made stone axes and miniature trapezoidal flint arrowheads; they cooked in clay
vessels without a potter’s wheel.
Hissar culture — a Late Neolithic culture (conventionally 7000-2000 BC) in the val-
leys of the Kafirnigan and Vakhsh rivers; an archaic culture of the tribes of the
foothills and the mountain valleys, which developed simultaneously with the more
developed settled-agricultural cultures (Anau, Jeitun).
The Bronze Age of Central Asia
The Bronze Age — the introduction of metallurgy: stone tools began to be replaced by
metal ones; irrigation (artificial irrigation) and urban planning appeared in the econ-
omy; the alloying of metals, embroidery/ornamentation, proto-urban settlements.
The Early Eneolithic (the 5th — the beginning of the 4th millennium BC): the growth
of the population of the foothills of the Kopet Dag; alongside small settlements of
0,5–1 hectares (Anau, Dashlyji, Yassy-depe) large centers of more than 10 hectares
arose (Kara-depe, Namazga-depe). The early agricultural tribes spread eastward to
the ancient delta of the Tejen (Gerirud) — the Geoksyur oasis.
The two pillars of the economy were agriculture and cattle breeding (livestock pro-
vided more than 4/5 of the meat consumed); pigs were also bred. The tools of the
Anau IA complex are massive stone hoes; in the Namazga I complex — ring stones
for hoe-like digging implements.
Bronze Age sites: Namazga I, Altyn-depe, Yalangach-depe, Mullali-depe, Kara-depe,
Zamanbaba (the area of Bukhara), Sapalli, Jarkutan.
Altyn-depe, Jarkutan and
Namazga-depe are Bronze Age sites and proto-urban settlements.
The art of the ancient period
The culture of the Early Eneolithic testifies to the growth of everyday prosperity:
almost a third of the clay pottery is painted with black paint on a red or yellowish
background.
In the Middle Eneolithic (the middle of the 4th millennium BC) the
unified culture of the early agricultural communities of southern Turkmenistan split
into a western and an eastern variant: the west is distinguished by multicoloured
painted ware with geometric ornament in a red-and-black scheme (Anau, Kara-depe,
Namazga-depe); in the east the ornaments are simpler and stricter — straight par-
allel lines along the rims of bowls and pots (Altyn-depe and the settlements of the
Geoksyur oasis).
Migrations to Central Asia and the transfer of information
The waves of migrations named in the lecture: the migrations of the Indo-European

3.2 3.2. Savollar — lecture questions with model answers
S1. What is civilization?
Answer.
Civilization is a complex human society, usually made up of cities, with
certain characteristics of cultural and technological development; an advanced state
of society with highly developed forms of government, culture, industry and common
social norms. The word comes from the Latin civitas — «city», so the basic definition
is «a society made up of cities». Early civilizations arose when people began to gather
in urban settlements; at the same time the criteria of being civilized are still disputed
because of the ethnocentric use of the term.
S2. What are the primary centers (sites) of Central Asian civilization?
Answer. Neolithic: Jeitun (southern Turkmenistan, 7200-4500 BC — the first agri-
culture), Kelteminar (5500-3500 BC, the deltas of the Amu Darya and the Zeravshan
— settled fishers with huge communal houses), the Hissar culture (the valleys of
the Kafirnigan and the Vakhsh).
Bronze Age:
Anau, Namazga-depe, Kara-depe,
Altyn-depe, the Geoksyur oasis, Yalangach-depe and Mullali-depe, Zamanbaba (the
Bukhara oasis), Sapalli and Jarkutan — proto-urban centers with metallurgy and ir-
rigation.
S3. What achievements were made in the Bronze Age?
Answer. The introduction of metallurgy — stone tools began to be replaced by metal
ones; the development of artificial irrigation; the appearance of urban planning and
proto-cities (Altyn-depe, Jarkutan, Namazga-depe); the growth of settlements (large
centers of more than 10 hectares); a two-pillar economy — agriculture and cattle
breeding; the development of applied art: painted pottery, geometric ornaments;
the differentiation of the cultures into western and eastern variants.
S4. What are the distinguishing indicators between the Neolithic and the
Bronze Age?
Answer. Neolithic (the 6th–5th millennia BC): the Neolithic Revolution — the transi-
tion to settled life, agriculture, cattle breeding, fishing, house building, early crafts,
pottery without metallurgy; stone tools. Bronze Age: metallurgy (the replacement
of stone by metal), irrigation, urban planning and proto-cities, further social strat-
ification and the greater complexity of the settlements, the painted pottery of two
schools. The key marker of the boundary is the appearance of metal and of cities.
S5. What do you know about the migrations to Central Asia?
Answer. The lecture singles out the waves: Indo-Europeans — Iranian tribes and
Indians; Jews; Turkic tribes (their penetration in the 4th–6th centuries); the Arabs in
the 7th–8th centuries (the bringing of Islam and subordination to the Arab Caliphate
from 704); the Mongols (the 13th century). Each wave mixed with the local popula-
tion, formed diasporas and strengthened tolerance; the migrants brought languages,
technologies and forms of economy.

4.1 4.1. Key points (the “all the rules” of the week)
The Concept of Statehood
The history of statehood — the formation of political entities, the transformation
of adats and tribal-clan forms into definite legal structures under a specific ruler
and system.
Tribal-clan forms — control over a territory with limited regulation;
transformation into statehood — the unification of different peoples and tribes on the
basis of a more developed legal process. Statehood on the territory of Uzbekistan
developed for about 3000 years; the first sprouts appeared in Khorezm (Khwarazm)
after the development of urban construction. The history of statehood is divided into
sovereign and dependent periods; the form of statehood was mostly a monarchy until
1920, therefore it is studied in the chronological order of dynasties.
A state — a political entity of society created according to definite rules. Modern
statehood — a way of the political organisation of ”society”; the state — the main
agent forming the representation of society; nation-states — the organisation of peo-
ple and territory into formally comparable sovereign governing units.
The emer-
gence of statehood in the world goes back to the Chalcolithic (the Copper-Stone
Age) in Egypt and Mesopotamia (the IV-III millennia BC). In the formation of states,
both autochthonous (local) and externally created ones are encountered.
The Six Periods of the Ancient Statehood of Turkestan
The 1st period: the development of early state forms in Northern Bactria in the
second half of the II millennium BC. The 2nd: the beginning of the I millennium
BC — the end of the VI century BC — the formation of the states of Bactria, Sogd
and Khorezm.
The 3rd: the early V century BC — 329 BC — the control of the
Achaemenids. The 4th: the end of the IV century — the end of the II century BC —
the coexistence of the Hellenistic states, Khorezm and Kangju (Kangüy). The 5th:
the end of the II century BC — the I century AD — the Kushan kingdom. The 6th: the
I-III centuries — the development and growth of ancient statehood, its final stage in
antiquity.
The Primary States
Turkestan — a special historical-geographical and historical-cultural region, where
civilisations existed for millennia thanks to two great rivers — the Amu Darya and
the Syr Darya.
Bactria: present-day Afghanistan, the south of Uzbekistan and Tajikistan; the capital
is Bactra. In the second half of the II millennium BC proto-cities arose here, which
later consolidated into the Ancient Bactrian kingdom; in the VI century it was oc-
cupied by the Achaemenids, then by Alexander the Great; later — the capital of the
Greco-Bactrian kingdom, until the Tocharians came.
Sogd: central Uzbekistan; the capital — present-day Samarkand. In the VI-IV cen-
turies BC — a satrapy of the Achaemenids; in 329 BC it was attacked by Alexander
the Great and conquered two years later.
Khorezm: it developed on the territory of present-day Khorezm; in the VII century
— the centre of Great Khorezm. At the end of the VI century BC it was occupied by

the Achaemenids, but Alexander the Great did not attack it — its ruler was wise in
foreign policy; it preserved its independence until the Arab conquest.
Dayuan: a state of the Fergana Valley; Zhang Qian noted 70 large and small cities.
Forms of States and Titles of Rulers
By genetic structure, states are divided into autochthonous (Kangju, Khorezmia) and
externally created (the Achaemenid Empire, the Greco-Bactrian kingdom). By typol-
ogy: a kingdom with the form of government ”absolute monarchy” (the Achaemenids,
Greco-Bactria); a theocratic monarchy — the Kushan kingdom; a confederative king-
dom with a limited monarchy — Kangju (no fewer than 5 possessions and the Great
Yuezhi); a domain — the hereditary power of tribal leaders and heads of clans.
Titles of rulers: the Indian factor — Bago pauro (”Son of God”) in Bactria; the Iranian
factor — shahanshah (”king of kings”); kavi — good princes; satar — the ruler of a
region or country; dakhi — ”lord of all regions”; yabgu — a ruler (a Turkic title);
amir; sultan; khan; emperor. The appearance of the title ”amir” is connected with
the Islamic system of governance; ”khan” came with the Turks; dynasties sought
legitimacy by tracing their lineage to Genghis Khan for the sake of the title of khan.
Medieval Statehood
The IV-VI centuries — the penetration of the Turks, migrations; the military raids of
the Chionites under the leadership of Grumbates; Sogdian coins with the image of an
archer and the word kydr (Kidara); the Hephthalites — from the middle of the V to the
middle of the VI century squeezed between Sasanid Iran and the Turks; the murder
of the Turkic ambassador on the territory of the Hephthalites; the joint attacks of the
Turkic Khaganate and the Sasanids liquidated the power of the Hephthalites.
Khorezm as an independent country was created by Afrig in the IV century (the Af-
rigid dynasty). The VI — early VIII centuries — the period under the Turkic Kha-
ganate. The year 704 — the beginning of the Arab attacks on Central Asia and of the
subordination to the Arab Caliphate.
Dynasty-states: the Samanids, Karakhanids, Ghaznavids, Seljuks, Khwarazmshahs,
Timurids.
The System of Governance of the Samanids (important for tests!)
The head of the state — the emir (Amir); the provinces were governed by governors
appointed by him. Together with the royal court (dargah — legislation and the judicial
system), ten centralised military-civilian departments (diwans) operated.
The main diwan — the diwan of the vizier: it controlled all the administrative, political
and economic institutions. The diwan of the mustawfi — financial affairs. The diwan
of amid al-mulk — diplomatic relations and the most important state papers. The
diwan of sahib ash-shurta — the royal guard and military affairs. The diwan of sahib
al-barid — the state post and the secret surveillance of local rulers and officials. The
diwan of the muhtasib — markets, measures and weights, trade, later public morals.
The diwan of the mushrif — the control of revenues and expenditures and other state
affairs. Also the diwans of judicial affairs, state lands and waqf (charitable) lands; in
the localities — organs of all the diwans.
The Timurids
Timur besieged Balkh: the fortifications were breached, Amir Husayn was defeated,
and on 10 April 1370 Timur came to power. He proclaimed the Chinggisids Suyur-
gatmish and Sultan Mahmud titular khans — an example of a limited monarchy, of
the monarch as a symbol of the unity of the nation.

Amir Timur conducted military campaigns to strengthen the empire: the army oc-
cupied 10 million sq. km — from Eastern Turkestan to the Mediterranean Sea in
the west, from Siberia to the Indian Ocean. The last great design was the campaign
against China, interrupted by the death of the ”conqueror of the world” in 1405 at
the age of 70.
From the Shaybanids to the Khanates
The division into small states: the Shaybanids, Ashtarkhanids, the Bukhara Emirate,
the Khanate of Khiva, the Khanate of Kokand. It was precisely these three states
(Bukhara, Khiva, Kokand) that were conquered by the Russian Empire in the second
half of the XIX century.
The National-Territorial Delimitation of 1924 and ”Nation-building”
In the 1920s, after the world war, the revolutions and the national movements, there
came the era of purposeful nation-building. The Soviet state created five republics
in stages: the Kazakh, Kirghiz, Uzbek, Tajik and Turkmen ones.
The pan-Turkic
dream of the Jadids of a single Turanian state with a single language was shattered
into five national states, of which four are Turkic-speaking and one (Tajikistan) is
Persian-speaking. The principles of ”language nationalism” were applied: to define
a territory by language and the supposed common history, to name the population
a single people and give it a single state. This operation is known as the national-
territorial delimitation of 1924.
Exceptions to the principles:
Kazakhstan consisted of Kazakhs and Russians in
roughly equal shares, and both were minorities — this is an example of a ”titular na-
tionality”; in Uzbekistan the Karakalpak Autonomous Republic was set apart for a dif-
ferent language, in Tajikistan — Badakhshan; important minorities remained in each
republic. The Soviet system promoted the Turkic languages and Tajik into modern
languages, ensured universal literacy and administrative use; it was accompanied by
”korenizatsiya” — the preferment of local cadres in party and state structures. The
new nations were built from above and from below, but without sovereignty — under
the ideological homogenisation of the CPSU; the party leaders became the national
leaders of the republics, which in 1991 turned the republics into nation-states.
Border-Making Terms (Central Asian Nations & Border Issues)
The terminology of boundary establishment: treaty, delimitation, demarcation, de-
lineation.
Treaty: according to Article 102 of the UN Charter — a general term for all instru-
ments binding under international law concluded between two or more international
legal persons, regardless of their formal designation. The Vienna Convention (1969):
”an international agreement concluded between states in written form and governed
by international law, embodied in one or several related instruments, whatever its
particular designation”.
Delimitation — a legal process in which two sovereign states establish and describe
in writing the location of their common border, mostly as a result of decision-making
at the negotiating table. Demarcation — a field operation: the marking of the po-
sition of the border on the ground so that it is visible to everyone; it begins with
topographic surveying; the goal is to establish physical signs that accurately repre-
sent the delimited border. Delineation — the graphic or mathematical representation
of the border; often one and the same joint commission conducts both demarcation
and delineation.

Uzbekistan–Kazakhstan negotiations: the longest borders of Uzbekistan; settlements
crossed by the border without inviolable areas in the north of the Tashkent and
Syrdarya regions; different chosen paths of development (protectionism — Uzbek-
istan, liberalisation — Kazakhstan). Negotiations with Kyrgyzstan: borders through
the most densely populated regions — the Tashkent, Namangan, Andijan and Fer-
gana regions; three enclaves of Uzbekistan; disputes and confrontations in the water
sphere.
The benefits of solving delimitation: stable and mutually agreed borders on the ba-
sis of international norms, the development of transit, partnership in the strategic
sectors — energy, agriculture, industry. The research hypotheses: H1 ”win–win” —
stable borders serve the prosperity of mutual relations; H2 — a reliable border policy
can make the country a centre for discussing problems at the international level. The
methods: policy analysis, discussions in social media, surveys, comparative analysis,
the systems approach; an obstacle — part of the archival materials is still secret.
The proposals: joint institutes of strategic research, benefits for entrepreneurs, new
methods of delimitation policy, the opening of transport corridors, mutual support of
the inviolability of borders, funds for joint scientific projects.

Answer. The state — a political entity of society created according to definite rules:
the unification of peoples and tribes under a more developed legal process, in con-
trast to tribal-clan forms with their limited regulation (adats). The modern state —
the main agent of organising society and territory into sovereign governed units; it
not only traditionally governs, but also produces laws regulating power over terri-

5.1 5.1. Key points (the “all the rules” of the week)
Uzbekistan under Soviet Power
The USSR sought to create a legal basis for the sovereign rights of the national re-
publics, which existed only conceptually: the constitution of 1924 proclaimed the vol-
untary principle of the federal structure of the USSR; the constitution of the Uzbek
SSR (March 1927) declared the republic an equal-in-rights and sovereign component
of the USSR. The government was headed by Fayzulla Khodjayev, who strove to ad-
vance the interests of the local population: the share of Uzbeks in the central organs
grew from 23% to 32.3% (1924–1928), at the lower levels of the state apparatus it
reached 75% by the end of 1930; the use of the Uzbek language in record-keeping
expanded.
However, the USSR methodically intensified hyper-centralisation: from the end of
the 1920s to the middle of the 1930s a totalitarian administrative model with the
ideologisation of the economy and a rigid centralisation of governance took root
in Uzbekistan. From the 1920s to the 1990s the region existed as a raw-material
appendage: the centuries-old dynastic statehood was replaced by ”nation-building”
states that sowed ethnic conflicts; the characteristic features of the period — repres-
sion, the cult of personality, the absence of private entrepreneurship, the suppression
of freedom of speech.
Collectivisation and Industrialisation
The curtailment of the NEP and the return to the methods of ”war communism” cre-
ated a bureaucratic command system of governing society.
In the second half of
the 1930s the dictatorship of Stalin established itself: the soviets became a decora-
tion of the party’s monopoly on power, the party and the state merged into a single
apparatus, the institutions of civil society were destroyed, and they were replaced
by pseudo-social organisations.
The ideological justification of global coercion —
Stalin’s formula about the sharpening of the class struggle on the path to socialism.
Collectivisation was carried out forcibly: dehkans were driven into kolkhozes under
the threat of deprivation of land, water and food; those who resisted were ”dekulak-
ized” — their property was confiscated and they were deported. In1930 −1933, 40 000
dehkan households were ”dekulakized” and 31 700 dehkans repressed (deportation
to 17 special settlements or beyond the borders of the republic — to the North Cau-
casus, Ukraine, Siberia); by 1933 more than 5 500 kulak families had been deported
beyond the borders of the republic; in the course of the ”cleansing” of the kolkhozes
of ”class enemies” more than 60 000 further dehkans were repressed. The ruin of
agriculture caused a famine that ended only in 1935.

The cotton monoculture: in 1933 cotton accounted for 81.5% of all the agricultural
produce of the republic, by 1937 — 93.4%; in 1940 Uzbekistan supplied 63% of the
all-union cotton, which ”freed the USSR from cotton imports” (in 1925 the USSR
imported 103 100 tonnes of cotton, by 1932 — only 24 300 tonnes). The positive
side: by 1940 gross agricultural output had grown by 130% relative to 1924, the
sown areas +50%, the livestock from 734 000 to 1 693 100, the tractors from a few
to 24 200.
The Four Phases of Soviet Repression in Uzbekistan (mandatory table!)
Phase 1 — the 1920s — early 1930s: the rollback from the NEP; the victims — re-
sistance, the national intelligentsia, politicians of alternative forms of development.
Accused of nationalism: K. Atabayev, T. Ryskulov, A. Rahimbaev, N. Tyurakulov, I.
Khidiraliyev, S. Khodzhanov; the cases of Inogamov, the ”Group of 18”, Kasymov
were fabricated; at the end of 1929 the members of the underground ”Milliy Istiqlol”
headed by the philosopher Munavvar Qari were arrested (85 people: 15 shot, the
rest — to the camps); the members of ”Milliy E’tiqod” (Mannan Ramiz, Nasir Saidov,
Batu, Hosil Vosilov, Sobir Kadyrov) were sentenced to death or to long terms.
Phase 2 — 1936–1939 (”The Great Terror”): the cases of Fayzulla Khodjayev (chair-
man of the Council of People’s Commissars), A. Ikramov (first secretary of the Cen-
tral Committee of the CP(b) of Uzbekistan), S. Segizbayev, A. Karimov, A. Islamov,
M. Tursunkhodjayev were fabricated — all were shot. By the spring of 1938 more
than 70% of the leaders of the republic had been repressed. In 1937-1939 alone
the ”troikas” of the NKVD (tribunals for ”counter-revolutionaries”) imprisoned more
than 41 000 people, of whom 6 920 were shot. The national intelligentsia was de-
stroyed: Abdulla Qodiriy, Abdulhamid Chulpon, Abdurauf Fitrat, Shakir Sulayman,
Ziya Said, Elbek, Agzam Ayub, Usman Nasyr, Kasym Sorokin, Muhammad Hasan, Ab-
dusalom Niyazi, Atojan Hashimov. The first Uzbek professor of history, Pulat Saliev,
was killed. In total, in 1937–1953 almost 100 000 people were repressed, of whom
13 000 were shot.
Phase 3 — 1946–1953: repression against the intelligentsia, financiers and partici-
pants of the war (until the death of Stalin).
Phase 4 — 1983–1985 (the ”Cotton Affair” / ”Uzbek Affair”, only for Uzbekistan): a
campaign of ”socialist cleansing” and of the struggle against corruption, in which
the blame for economic failures was placed on local cadres; the mass media of the
USSR presented corruption as having engulfed the whole nation, which insulted na-
tional dignity. The investigative groups of Gdlyan and Ivanov applied the methods of
Stalin and Beria: beatings, unlawful arrests; in total more than 25 000 leaders and
economic managers of Uzbekistan were arrested.
Literacy and Deculturation
The contrasts of the epoch: literacy grew from ~{}11% (1928) to 68% (1939); in
1940 — 5 504 general-education schools and 1 368 800 pupils (against 82 300 in
1924); compulsory primary education was introduced and the transition to universal
seven-year schooling began; in 1928 industry had 1 400 engineers and technicians,
by 1940 — 6 000; as of 1 January 1941 the republic had 55 300 specialists with
diplomas (20 200 with higher and 35 100 with secondary specialised education).
The negative side: the change of writing systems led to a new wave of illiteracy;
private schools were liquidated; prison terms of 10–15 years for publication in the
Arabic script; the imposition of Soviet rites; the harm of accelerated ”international-
isation”; the curtailment of the appointment of national cadres; a culture ”socialist
in content, internationalist in spirit, national in form”; the alienation of the people

from their thousand-year spiritual heritage and the destruction of historical memory.
Language policy: in 1938 — the compulsory study of Russian in national schools (a
reduction of the hours of the native language); in 1940 the Cyrillic script was intro-
duced by decree; Russian was raised to the level of the state language.
Migrations and Centralisation
A policy of the artificial increase of the multinational composition of the republics:
forced and uncontrolled voluntary resettlement. The first deported — the Koreans
of the Far East, the Germans of the Volga region, the Poles of western Ukraine and
Belorussia.
Between September and December 1937 more than 74 500 Koreans
arrived in Uzbekistan.
In 1943-1944 — political exiles from the North Caucasus,
from Georgia and from Crimea: about 110 000 Meskhetian Turks from Georgia and
151 424 Crimean Tatars from Crimea.
Uzbekistan remained strictly subordinate to the centre: under Article 17(c) even the
establishment of borders and the division of regions into districts were subject to
approval by the Supreme Soviet of the USSR.
The Contribution to the Victory over Fascism (figures for tests!)
1 433 230 people took part in the war — more than 40% of the able-bodied population
of the republic; 263 005 were killed, 132 670 went missing in action, 395 795 did not
return, 60 452 became invalids. About 120 000 soldiers were awarded orders and
medals; the title of Hero of the Soviet Union was received by 280 people, of whom
75 were Uzbeks.
Industry was put on a war footing; more than 100 enterprises were evacuated and
housed from Russia, Ukraine and Belorussia. More than 1 million evacuees from
the occupied districts were received, including 200 000 children; orphanages were
opened, and many children were adopted by Uzbek families. During the war years
two volumes on the life and work of Alisher Navoi were published, together with
works of the classics (Lutfi, Bedil) and the poems ”Shirin and Shakar”, ”Kunduz and
Yolduz”, ”Dalli”, ”Muradkhan”, ”Malika ayor”; creative work was done by Aibek, Ay-
din, S. Ahmad, Hamid Alimjan, Gafur Ghulam, Mirtemir, Shaykhzade, Zulfiya and
others.
After Stalin: the Losses of the Republic
De-Stalinisation and the rehabilitation of the victims of political genocide; the general
approach to national policy changed little. The important role of Sharaf Rashidov;
from the 1960s to the early 1980s dozens of large industrial enterprises were opened:
by 1985, 1 549 enterprises of machine-building, chemistry, construction, light indus-
try and the agro-industrial branches were functioning; irrigation canals — 197 000
km, 23 reservoirs for 10 billion cubic metres of water.
The losses: the specialisation of a raw-material supplier; in the 1980s the annual
deliveries of gas exceeded 250 billion cubic metres, of gold — more than 50 tonnes; a
continuous flow of cobalt, molybdenum, tungsten, refined copper, uranium; minerals
worth ~{}5.5 billion dollars a year. The revenues from the sale of gold and rare
metals did not reach the treasury of Uzbekistan: in the last 15 years of the USSR,
”cotton and gold” worth no less than 35 billion dollars were taken away for the needs
of the centre, and the total value of the minerals delivered to the central regions
exceeded 75 billion dollars. The cotton monoculture and the uncontrolled use of the
waters of the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya led to the tragedy of the Aral Sea.
Perestroika and the Path to Independence

”Perestroika”, proclaimed by M. Gorbachev in April 1985 — the hope of an exit from
the systemic crisis; the ”new thinking” in foreign policy for the sake of ”universal
human values” and ”a world without violence and war”. National movements were
born with demands for democratic reform and genuine sovereignty, for the rebirth
of national consciousness and the restoration of national statehood.
The wave of
demonstrations of 1989 swept through Fergana, Kokand, Kuvasay, Gulistan, Parkent
and Buka.
Islam Karimov, elected president at the first session of the XII convocation of the
Supreme Soviet of the Uzbek SSR (March 1990) — an unprecedented step: before
this, not a single union region had elected a president; the centre reacted extremely
negatively. The idea of political sovereignty and economic self-reliance was advanced
as the decisive conditions of independence: in 1989 the Uzbek language was given
the status of the state language; measures were taken to liquidate the cotton mono-
culture and to restore spirituality; August 1989 — the resolution on personal sub-
sidiary plots; the beginning of 1990 — the employment programme; July 1990 — the
decree on improving the water supply and the gasification of the countryside.
The ”Declaration of Independence” was adopted at the second session of the
Supreme Soviet of Uzbekistan (18–20 June 1990, XII convocation; 12 articles). It
enshrined: the supremacy of the democratic state and of the laws throughout the
whole territory; the independent resolution of internal and foreign-policy questions;
the recognition of and respect for the basic principles of international law; the de-
termination of one’s own path of development, and more.
19 August 1991 — the last attempt to preserve the USSR: an unconstitutional coup
d’état, the creation of the GKChP (State Committee for the State of Emergency),
the isolation of Gorbachev; the visit of I. Karimov to India was interrupted.
The
emergency 6th session of the XII convocation adopted the Statement of the Supreme
Soviet on the independence of Uzbekistan and the Law ”On the Foundations of the
State Independence of the Republic of Uzbekistan”. 31 August 1991 — independence
was proclaimed; by the resolution ”On the Proclamation of the State Independence
of the Republic of Uzbekistan” 1 September was declared Independence Day and a
day off beginning with 1991.
The textbook adds: the referendum on independence (a test of the people’s support)
and the first nationwide elections of the President; the Constitutional Law ”On the
Foundations of State Independence”, the state symbols (emblem, flag, anthem) and
the national currency — the basic attributes of sovereignty (topic 4 of the textbook).
5.2 5.2. Savollar — lecture questions with model answers
S1.
What was the main idea behind the creation of new republics in the
Soviet Union?
Answer. The idea of nation-building: the creation of national republics on the linguis-
tic principle in order to build ”homo sovieticus” — a person who thinks, behaves and
lives in the Soviet way. Peoples living in one locality were separated by languages;
instead of centuries-old traditions, moderate ”Soviet” values were imposed with a
preference for the traditions of non-Muslim societies; the republics were created
without sovereignty, under the ideological homogenisation of the CPSU.
S2. Why did the Soviet Union pursue a harsh repressive policy?
Answer. Repression was an instrument of building homo sovieticus and of suppress-
ing any resistance: physical reprisal against the intelligentsia and influential people
facilitated the ”watering” of Soviet ideology; intimidation maintained the loyalty of

repression (the 1920s — early 1930s; 1936–1939 ”The Great Terror”; 1946–1953;

S3. What was the main contribution of the population of Uzbekistan to the

Answer. 1 433 230 conscripted (more than 40% of the able-bodied), 263 005 killed,
132 670 missing in action, 395 795 who did not return, 60 452 invalids; ~{}120

evacuated enterprises; the reception of more than 1 million evacuees, including 200

S4. What was the intellectual and scientific development in the Soviet pe-
riod?
Answer. Contradictory: the growth of literacy from 11% to 68% (1928-1939), a net-
work of schools (5 504 in 1940), specialists (55 300 by 1941), high poetry, drama and
prose inspired by the Jadids (Aibek, Alimjan, Gafur Ghulam, Mirtemir, Shaykhzade);
the Academy of Sciences was opened in the war years because of the evacuation of
scholars. But: the persecution of the intelligentsia, the change of alphabets, prison
terms for the Arabic script, ideological contradiction, the destruction of the school
of history (the arrest of the first professor of history, Pulat Saliev).
S5. How were the natural resources of Uzbekistan distributed for the people
of Uzbekistan?
Answer. The republic was not the real master of its resources: all the revenue from
gas, gold and rare metals was controlled by the union centre. In the 1980s: gas
> 250 billion cubic metres and gold > 50 tonnes annually; minerals worth ~{}5.5
billion dollars a year; in the last 15 years of the USSR, ”cotton and gold” worth 35+
billion and minerals worth 75+ billion dollars were taken out — while Uzbekistan
was criticised for corruption and low productivity. The revenues did not enter the
treasury of the republic.
S6. What changes took place in the period of perestroika?
Answer.
April 1985 — the proclamation of perestroika by Gorbachev and the
”new thinking”; glasnost weakened the ideological yoke; national movements for
sovereignty were born; the demonstrations of 1989 (Fergana, Kokand, Kuvasay,
Gulistan, Parkent, Buka); the election of I. Karimov as president (March 1990); the
Uzbek language — the state language (1989); the Declaration of Independence (June
1990, 12 articles); the GKChP on 19 August 1991 and the proclamation of indepen-
dence on 31 August 1991.
